question: What do we call an abnormal, new growth of tissue that forms a tumor?
explanation: Great start! A neoplasm is simply an abnormal mass of tissue that grows when cells divide more than they should. Think 'neo' (new) + 'plasma' (formation). You've got this! [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: What happens when the chemical signals that control normal cell division break down?
explanation: Spot on! When the body's natural brakes on the cell cycle fail, cells lose their stop signals and keep dividing, leading to abnormal growth. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of these is the main feature of a benign tumor?

options.A: It travels through the blood to distant organs
options.C: It remains localized and does not spread

explanation: You got it! Benign tumors stay put in one place. They don't invade nearby tissues or spread around the body like malignant ones do. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What does it mean when a cancer cell is called 'poorly differentiated'?

options.A: The cancer cells look very different from normal tissue cells
options.B: The tumor cells have stopped growing completely
options.C: The cells are surrounded by a thick protective capsule
options.D: The mass is unable to attract a blood supply

explanation: Well done! 'Differentiated' means looking like the original tissue. Poorly differentiated cells have lost their specialized look, which usually means the cancer is more aggressive. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h2)

question: What is the normal job of tumor suppressor genes in our bodies?

options.A: To stimulate rapid cell growth during injury
options.B: To supply blood vessels directly to growing tissues
options.C: To carry oxygen to rapidly dividing cancer cells
options.D: To slow down cell division and repair damaged DNA

explanation: Exactly! Think of tumor suppressor genes as the body's molecular brakes. They pause cell growth to fix DNA mistakes or clear out damaged cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: How do normal proto-oncogenes cause trouble when they mutate?

options.A: They permanently shut down all cellular activity in the organ
options.B: They cause the immune system to destroy healthy tissue
options.C: They stop the tumor from getting a blood supply
options.D: They become overactive oncogenes that drive constant cell division

explanation: Spot on! When proto-oncogenes mutate, they turn into hyperactive oncogenes that act like a stuck accelerator pedal, shouting for the cell to multiply nonstop. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which phase of cancer development involves a permanent change or mutation in a cell's DNA?
explanation: You nailed it! Initiation is always step one—it's the very first moment a trigger causes a permanent genetic change in a normal cell. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the main job of promoting agents during the second stage of cancer?

options.A: To help the immune system destroy early cancer cells
options.B: To stimulate previously mutated cells to divide and multiply
options.C: To stop blood vessels from growing into the tumor
options.D: To cause the initial DNA damage inside the cell nucleus

explanation: Correct! Promoters don't start the mutation themselves, but they act like fertilizer, encouraging those already-mutated cells to multiply and grow. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is the term for the process where a tumor grows its own new blood supply?
explanation: Awesome! 'Angio' (vessels) + 'genesis' (creation). Tumors rely on angiogenesis to build their own private network of blood vessels to keep growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: Why is angiogenesis so important for a growing malignant tumor?

options.A: It supplies necessary oxygen and nutrients while removing waste
options.B: It prevents the immune system from noticing the tumor mass
options.C: It encapsulates the tumor to keep it from spreading locally
options.D: It repairs damaged DNA inside the fast-growing cancer cells

explanation: You got it! Without a fresh blood supply delivering nutrients and carrying away waste, a tumor would quickly starve and stop growing. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h5)

question: What do we call the spread of cancer cells to other parts of the body?
explanation: Fantastic! Metastasis is when cancer cells break away from the main tumor, travel through the body, and set up secondary tumor camps elsewhere. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: How do migrating cancer cells manage to break into nearby blood vessels?

options.A: They secrete enzymes that break down surrounding tissue barriers
options.B: They attract white blood cells to carry them into circulation
options.C: They wait for the blood vessel walls to rupture from high pressure
options.D: They shrink in size until they slip through normal cell walls

explanation: Spot on! Cancer cells release special chemical enzymes that chew through tissue barriers and blood vessel walls, letting them slip right into circulation. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which immune cells are on the front lines, patrolling tissues to destroy abnormal cells?
explanation: You got it! T-cells and natural killer (NK) cells are the heavy lifters of the immune system, constantly hunting down and destroying abnormal or infected cells. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)

question: How do malignant cells often manage to survive even when a healthy immune system is present?

options.A: They absorb all circulating antibodies to block inflammation
options.B: They coat themselves in thick layers of calcium and iron
options.C: They turn into benign tumors to trick white blood cells
options.D: They release chemical signals that suppress immune cell activity

explanation: Well done! Clever cancer cells can send out decoy signals that turn down immune responses, tricking the body's defenses into leaving them alone. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T2#GNS321_U1_T2_h7)
